answer.answerText:
Yes. For multiple occupancies, apply the applicable Table 403.1 fixture ratio or ratios separately to each occupancy and fixture type, then add the fractional results before rounding the combined result up to the next whole number. For sex-specific fixtures, the default is to divide each total occupant load equally between the sexes; a different distribution requires approved statistical data. For Group B office occupancies, the calculation uses the total occupant load on the given floor. Fixture minimums are those in Table 403.1, while the Building Code determines the occupancy classification and occupant load. If an occupancy type is not shown in Table 403.1, it must be considered individually by the commissioner.

The multipurpose room may use Assembly fixture requirements if it is actually used for assembly, has an occupant load under 75, and is accessory to another occupancy. In that circumstance, BC 303.1.3 classifies it as Group B or as part of the other occupancy, while expressly allowing its plumbing-fixture count to be calculated under the Assembly requirements. The separately supplied PC 403.1 permission concerns a building or nonaccessory tenant assembly space classified as Group B under the cited BC 303.1 exception; it is not independent authority for the potentially accessory room here.

A final fixture count cannot be determined on the supplied facts. The actual function and resulting Building-Code classification and occupant load of each space, the applicable Table 403.1 rows and Assembly category, the accessory relationship of the multipurpose room, and existing/proposed fixtures remain material. The selected evidence also does not establish permission for facilities to be shared among the identified occupancies.
answer.conclusion: Yes. For multiple occupancies, apply the applicable Table 403.1 fixture ratio or ratios separately to each occupancy and fixture type, then add the fractional results before rounding the combined result up to the next whole number. For sex-specific fixtures, the default is to divide each total occupant load equally between the sexes; a different distribution requires approved statistical data. For Group B office occupancies, the calculation uses the total occupant load on the given floor. Fixture minimums are those in Table 403.1, while the Building Code determines the occupancy classification and occupant load. If an occupancy type is not shown in Table 403.1, it must be considered individually by the commissioner.

1004.3 1004.3 Fixed seating. For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats. The occupant load of wheelchair spaces and the associated companion seat shall be based on one occupant for each wheelchair space and one occupant for the associated companion seat provided in accordance with Section 1108.2.3. For areas having fixed seating without dividing arms, the occupant load shall be not less than the number of seats based on one person for each 18 inches (457.2 mm) of seating length. The occupant load of seating booths shall be based on one person for each 24 inches (609.6 mm) of booth seat length measured at the backrest of the seating booth.

The interior corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be constructed as public corridors in accordance with Table 1020.1.2 with 1-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers, and 2-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers where a dead-end corridor exceeds 40 feet (12 192 mm) in length; 2. Access to the corridors shall be limited to those necessary for exit access through the corridor from normally occupied spaces. Direct openings from the mechanical, electrical and other storage spaces shall not be permitted, except that access to the corridor may be provided through a vestibule constructed with fire barriers, with a minimum fire-resistance rating consistent with the required hourly rating for the corridor; 3. Corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be sufficient to accommodate a total occupant load on the basis of 3 square feet (0.28 m 2 ) per person; 4. The minimum dimension of such corridors shall be sufficient to accommodate the total occupant load discharging into such corridors, but shall in no case be less than 5 feet (1524 mm) in minimum dimension; and 5. In addition to Conditions 1 through 4 above, one of the following conditions shall be met: 5.1. Each of the interior exit stairways and ramps serving such story shall be protected by a smokeproof enclosure in accordance with Section 909.20; 5.2. The corridor or portions of the corridor serving the rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall be pressurized in accordance with requirements that are applicable to interior exit stairways. Connecting interior exit stairways need not be pressurized unless otherwise required by this code; 5.3. All passenger elevators serving the rooms, areas, or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall comply with occupant self-evacuation elevator requirements in Section 3008.1 through 3008.11; or 5.4. One additional exit stairway meeting the requirements of Sections 1009 and 1023 shall be provided in addition to the minimum number of exits required by Section 1006 . The total width of any combination of remaining exit stairways with one exit stairway removed shall not be less than the total width required by Section 1005.3. Rooms, areas or spaces that do not comply with the conditions in Sections 1004.1.1.2.1 and 1004.1.1.2.2, or Section 1004.1.1.2.3 where applicable, shall have occupant loads calculated cumulatively per story and be classified as Occupancy Group A.

DWELLING UNIT. A single unit consisting of one or more habitable rooms and occupied or arranged to be occupied as a unit separate from all other units within a dwelling. EXIT ACCESS. That portion of a means of egress system that leads from any occupied portion of a building or structure to an exit. FOOD COURT. See Section 402.2. INTERIOR EXIT STAIRWAY. An exit component that serves to meet one or more means of egress design requirements, such as required number of exits or exit access travel distance, and provides for a protected path of egress travel to the exit discharge or public way. NURSING HOMES . See Section 308 . 2 . 2 . OCCUPANT LOAD . The number of persons for which the means of egress of a building or portion thereof is designed . PARKING GARAGE. A structure or portion of a structure, other than a private garage or carport, used for the parking or storage of motor vehicles. WHEELCHAIR SPACE . A space for a single wheelchair and its occupant .

403.2 403.2 Separate facilities. Where plumbing fixtures are required, separate facilities shall be provided for each sex. Exceptions: 1. Separate facilities shall not be required for dwelling units and sleeping units. 2. In structures or tenant spaces where combined employee and public toilet facilities are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of employees, customers, patrons and visitors is 30 or fewer. 3. In structures or tenant spaces where required toilet facilities for only employee use are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of employees is 30 or fewer. 4. In structures or tenant spaces where required toilet facilities for only public use are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of customers, patrons and visitors is 30 or fewer.
419.2 419.2 Substitution for water closets. In each bathroom or toilet room, urinals shall not be substituted for more than 50 percent of the required water closets.

403.2.1 403.2.1 Family or assisted-use toilet facilities serving as separate facilities. Where a building or tenant space requires a separate toilet facility for each sex and each toilet facility is required to have only one water closet, two-family* or assisted-use toilet facilities shall be permitted to serve as the required separate facilities. Family or assisted-use toilet facilities shall not be required to be identified for exclusive use by either sex as required by Section 403.4. (Am. projectContext.existingDocumentation: Group B floor documented at 1 occupant per 100 square feet
projectContext.reportedCalculatedLoad: More than 200 occupants overall, with no individual room at 75 or more
projectContext.proposedReduction: Count selected seats and treat some functions as nonsimultaneous

exactPassages: Where an area under consideration contains multiple functions having different occupant load factors, the design occupant load for such area shall be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

Where the actual number of occupants of any space will be significantly lower than listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the commissioner may establish a lower basis for the determination of the number of occupants.

For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats.

testCase.question: For this 2022-code evaluation scenario, may the conference floor's occupant load be documented by counting selected movable seats, omitting lounge and break functions as nonsimultaneous, and retaining the existing 1:100 load without a commissioner-established lower basis?
testCase.expectedConclusion: No. BC 1004.3 uses the number of installed seats for fixed seating, while areas without fixed seating must be determined under BC 1004.1.3. BC 1004.1.2 requires the floor area of each function with a different occupant-load factor to be calculated independently. A lower actual-occupancy basis is not automatic: BC 1004.1.3.1 states that the commissioner may establish it when actual occupancy will be significantly lower. The selected evidence does not establish that the lounge and break areas may be omitted as nonsimultaneous, nor does it resolve filing type, place-of-assembly status, posted occupancy, or egress capacity. Those conclusions require the actual plans, functions, use assumptions, existing records, and applicable official authority.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages reject automatic movable-seat counting and require independent functional calculations, but a final occupant load and any approved lower basis depend on missing plans, facts, and commissioner action.

answer.answerText:
No—not on the stated rationale. Because the seats are movable rather than fixed, the fixed-seat method does not apply. Each area without fixed seating must have an occupant load of at least its floor area divided by the Table 1004.1.3 factor for that space’s actual function. Where the floor contains functions with different factors, each function’s area must be calculated independently. Thus, selected movable-seat counts cannot replace the applicable area-factor calculation for conference, soft-seating, coffee-break, or lounge functions.

The supplied provisions also do not authorize omitting lounge or break areas merely by characterizing them as nonsimultaneous. For means of egress, the design occupant load is the largest load computed under the applicable calculation rules, subject only to the expressly referenced permissions. A lower basis is available only if the actual number of occupants will be significantly below the table result and the commissioner establishes that lower basis.

Accordingly, the existing 1:100 documentation may be retained only if it is at least the result required by independently applying the applicable Table 1004.1.3 factors to the actual functions and areas—or if a commissioner-established lower basis supports the reduction. The supplied evidence does not include Table 1004.1.3, so it cannot establish whether 1:100 is adequate for these proposed functions or produce a final floor load.
answer.conclusion: No—not on the stated rationale. Because the seats are movable rather than fixed, the fixed-seat method does not apply. Each area without fixed seating must have an occupant load of at least its floor area divided by the Table 1004.1.3 factor for that space’s actual function. Where the floor contains functions with different factors, each function’s area must be calculated independently. Thus, selected movable-seat counts cannot replace the applicable area-factor calculation for conference, soft-seating, coffee-break, or lounge functions.

supportedPoints.heading: Multiple functions require separate area calculations
supportedPoints.explanation: Where an area contains multiple functions having different occupant-load factors, the design occupant load must be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently. The proposed conference, soft-seating, coffee-break, and lounge uses therefore cannot be treated as one undifferentiated area if their applicable factors differ.

supportedPoints.heading: Movable seats do not establish the load for areas without fixed seating
supportedPoints.explanation: For an area without fixed seating, the occupant load must be no less than the floor area divided by the Table 1004.1.3 factor assigned to the space’s function. The stated movable seating is not fixed seating, so counting only selected movable seats does not satisfy this supplied minimum-calculation rule.

supportedPoints.heading: Seat count applies only to fixed seats, with nonfixed areas added
supportedPoints.explanation: The fixed-seat method applies to areas having fixed seats and aisles. It also requires areas without installed fixed seating, such as waiting spaces, to be calculated under BC 1004.1.3 and added to the fixed-seat count. This reinforces that the stated movable seats do not provide a fixed-seat basis.

supportedPoints.heading: A lower basis requires commissioner action
supportedPoints.explanation: Where actual occupancy will be significantly lower than the Table 1004.1.3 result, the commissioner may establish a lower basis. The supplied evidence does not authorize an applicant to adopt a lower basis without that commissioner-established determination.

supportedPoints.heading: Egress is designed for the largest applicable computed load
supportedPoints.explanation: For means-of-egress requirements, facilities must be provided for the largest number computed under BC 1004.1.3, unless an identified permission applies. The supplied evidence does not establish a permission to exclude otherwise applicable lounge or break areas simply because they are asserted to be nonsimultaneous.

sources.text: Where an area under consideration contains multiple functions having different occupant load factors, the design occupant load for such area shall be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

Where the actual number of occupants of any space will be significantly lower than listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the commissioner may establish a lower basis for the determination of the number of occupants.

For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats.

1004.1 1004.1 Design occupant load. Design occupant load. In determining means of egress requirements, the number of occupants for whom means of egress facilities shall be provided shall be established by the largest number computed in accordance with Section 1004.1.3, unless otherwise permitted by Section 1004.1.3.1, 1004.1.3.2 or 1004.2.

1004.1.3.2 1004.1.3.2 Unlisted functions. Where data regarding the square feet area per person for a function is not listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the occupant load shall be established by a registered design professional, subject to the approval of the commissioner.

1004.1.1.2.3 1004.1.1.2.3 Group R-2 accessory spaces as primary function on a story. Where the aggregate Group R-2 occupancy accessory area of all rooms, areas or spaces, including outdoor spaces that are not provided with independent means of egress and that do not converge into interior means of egress, exceed 50 percent of the building area of the story in which they are located, and the total number of occupants on such story exceeds 150 persons, the following conditions shall apply: 1. The interior corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be constructed as public corridors in accordance with Table 1020.1.2 with 1-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers, and 2-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers where a dead-end corridor exceeds 40 feet (12 192 mm) in length; 2. Access to the corridors shall be limited to those necessary for exit access through the corridor from normally occupied spaces. Direct openings from the mechanical, electrical and other storage spaces shall not be permitted, except that access to the corridor may be provided through a vestibule constructed with fire barriers, with a minimum fire-resistance rating consistent with the required hourly rating for the corridor; 3. Corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be sufficient to accommodate a total occupant load on the basis of 3 square feet (0.28 m 2 ) per person; 4. The minimum dimension of such corridors shall be sufficient to accommodate the total occupant load discharging into such corridors, but shall in no case be less than 5 feet (1524 mm) in minimum dimension; and 5. In addition to Conditions 1 through 4 above, one of the following conditions shall be met: 5.1. Each of the interior exit stairways and ramps serving such story shall be protected by a smokeproof enclosure in accordance with Section 909.20; 5.2. The corridor or portions of the corridor serving the rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall be pressurized in accordance with requirements that are applicable to interior exit stairways. Connecting interior exit stairways need not be pressurized unless otherwise required by this code; 5.3. All passenger elevators serving the rooms, areas, or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall comply with occupant self-evacuation elevator requirements in Section 3008.1 through 3008.11; or 5.4. One additional exit stairway meeting the requirements of Sections 1009 and 1023 shall be provided in addition to the minimum number of exits required by Section 1006 . The total width of any combination of remaining exit stairways with one exit stairway removed shall not be less than the total width required by Section 1005.3. Rooms, areas or spaces that do not comply with the conditions in Sections 1004.1.1.2.1 and 1004.1.1.2.2, or Section 1004.1.1.2.3 where applicable, shall have occupant loads calculated cumulatively per story and be classified as Occupancy Group A.

1004.1.1.2 1004.1.1.2 Cumulative occupant loads in Group R-2 occupancies. Rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to a Group R-2 occupancy and that comply with the conditions below may have occupant loads calculated individually per room, area, or space, and be classified as Occupancy Group R-2.

CERTIFICATE OF OPERATION. A certificate issued by the department upon satisfactory inspection of a specific piece of hoisting equipment to ensure that the equipment is in compliance with this code. DWELLING UNIT. A single unit consisting of one or more habitable rooms and occupied or arranged to be occupied as a unit separate from all other units within a dwelling. EXIT ACCESS. That portion of a means of egress system that leads from any occupied portion of a building or structure to an exit. FIXED SEATING. Furniture or fixture designed and installed for the use of sitting and secured in place including bench-type seats and seats with or without backs or arm rests. INTERIOR EXIT STAIRWAY. An exit component that serves to meet one or more means of egress design requirements, such as required number of exits or exit access travel distance, and provides for a protected path of egress travel to the exit discharge or public way. OCCUPANT LOAD . The number of persons for which the means of egress of a building or portion thereof is designed . PARKING GARAGE. A structure or portion of a structure, other than a private garage or carport, used for the parking or storage of motor vehicles. WHEELCHAIR SPACE . A space for a single wheelchair and its occupant .
402.8.2 402.8.2 Occupant load. The calculated occupant load used to determine the required number of means of egress shall be in accordance with this section.

303.7 303.7 Certificate of Operation. A Certificate of Operation shall be required, as per Section 28-117.1 , for the following assembly occupancies: 1. Indoor assembly occupancies used or intended for use by 75 persons or more, including open spaces at 20 feet (6096 mm) or more above or below grade plane, such as roofs or roof terraces. 2. Outdoor assembly occupancies used and intended for use by 200 persons or more. Section BC 304: Business Group B

1108.2.3 1108.2.3 Companion seats. At least one companion seat complying with ICC A117.1, including Section 802.7 (Companion Seat), shall be provided for each wheelchair space required by Sections 1108.2.2.1 through 1108.2.2.3 of this code.

testCase.title: Legacy fire-alarm system scope after a Group B enlargement

projectContext.project: Building enlargement with no stated use or occupancy change
unknowns: highest occupied-floor height above Fire Department vehicle access
whether any occupancy classification or usage changes

exactPassages: Additions, alterations, renovations or repairs to existing systems shall conform to that required for new systems without requiring the existing system to comply with all of the requirements of this code, except as otherwise required in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. Additions, alterations or repairs shall not cause an existing installation to become unsafe, hazardous or overloaded.
Fire protection systems governed by this chapter shall be provided:
1. To the entire building as if the building were hereafter erected, where a change is made in the main use or dominant occupancy of such building.
2. Throughout a space, where a change is made in the occupancy group classification or usage of the space.
selectedEvidence.resolvedTitle: 901.9.2 Additional requirements based on change of occupancy or use.

exactPassages: Fire protection systems shall be provided in enlarged portions of a building and where this chapter would require such systems in new construction for a space or building.

Group B occupancies having a total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet (9290.3 m 2 ) located in buildings where the highest occupied floor is 75 feet (22 860 mm) or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access shall be provided with automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire alarm system in accordance with Section 907.2.13.1 and an emergency voice/alarm communication system in accordance with Section 907.5.2.2 that initiates a total evacuation signal.

testCase.question: An existing prior-code Group B building has a previously approved legacy fire-alarm system. A proposed enlargement does not change the stated use or occupancy, but the resulting Group B gross area may exceed 100,000 square feet. The height of the highest occupied floor above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access has not been confirmed. Does the selected 2022 Building Code evidence automatically require replacement of the entire legacy system, and what additional facts determine the required scope?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The enlargement does not, by itself, prove that the entire legacy system must be replaced. BC 901.9.1 requires additions and alterations to existing systems to comply with new-system requirements without automatically requiring the entire existing system to comply, subject to the additional triggers in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. BC 901.9.3 requires fire-protection systems in enlarged portions and where Chapter 9 would require them for new construction. If the resulting Group B occupancy exceeds 100,000 square feet and the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, BC 907.2.2.2 requires the identified smoke-detection, fire-alarm, and emergency voice/alarm systems for the qualifying Group B occupancy; that requirement cannot automatically be limited to only the enlarged portion. On the stated facts, BC 901.9.2 is not triggered unless the asserted absence of an occupancy or use change is incorrect. A main-use or dominant-occupancy change applies to the entire building; a space occupancy-classification or usage change applies throughout that space. The selected evidence does not determine whether the legacy equipment can be extended, interfaced, or retained, or whether technical conditions ultimately require modification or replacement.

answer.answerText:
No. On the stated facts, the selected evidence does not automatically require replacement of the entire previously approved legacy fire-alarm system. Additions, alterations, renovations, or repairs to an existing system must meet the requirements for new systems, but the existing system need not be made fully compliant with the 2022 Code unless one of the additional provisions in BC 901.9.2 through 901.9.6 applies. The work also cannot make the existing installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

For the enlargement, systems are required in the enlarged portion and wherever Chapter 9 would require them in new construction for a space or building. If the resulting Group B occupancy exceeds 100,000 gross square feet **and** the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access, BC 907.2.2.2 requires automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire-alarm system and an emergency voice/alarm communication system that initiates a total-evacuation signal. This is a building/occupancy new-construction trigger in addition to the enlarged-portion rule; the supplied text does not authorize confining that required system to only the enlargement.

The stated absence of a use or occupancy change means the supplied change-of-use provisions do not currently establish a broader retrofit. But a change in main use or dominant occupancy would require Chapter 9 systems throughout the building as if newly erected; a change in a space's occupancy-group classification or usage would require them throughout that space.

There is also a separate potential whole-building path for this prior-code building. If completed work increases floor surface area by more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area, the entire building must comply as if newly erected. Floor surface area includes the gross square footage of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces at every level, including cellar, attic, roof, bulkheads, and superstructures. In calculating the existing area for that threshold, exclude: (1) floors removed during the work together with their supporting beams, joists, decking, and slabs on grade; and (2) floors installed with those supporting elements less than 12 months before submission of the construction-document approval application—including floors installed under a work permit signed off less than 12 months before that submission. Exceeding 100,000 square feet alone does not establish this separate 110-percent trigger.

The final fire-alarm scope therefore remains unresolved. It depends at minimum on the confirmed post-work Group B gross area, the highest-occupied-floor measurement, the precise enlargement and fire-alarm modification scope, whether any use or classification changes occur, whether the 110-percent floor-surface-area rule applies, and whether the approved legacy system has the capacity and compatibility to provide any required new functions without unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded conditions. The selected evidence establishes the large-area functions, but does not establish detector locations or quantity, equipment specifications, wiring, voice coverage, or complete system-design requirements.

The work also cannot make the existing installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

Fire protection systems governed by this chapter shall be provided:
1. To the entire building as if the building were hereafter erected, where a change is made in the main use or dominant occupancy of such building.
2. Throughout a space, where a change is made in the occupancy group classification or usage of the space.
Fire protection systems shall be provided in enlarged portions of a building and where this chapter would require such systems in new construction for a space or building.

Group B occupancies having a total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet (9290.3 m 2 ) located in buildings where the highest occupied floor is 75 feet (22 860 mm) or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access shall be provided with automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire alarm system in accordance with Section 907.2.13.1 and an emergency voice/alarm communication system in accordance with Section 907.5.2.2 that initiates a total evacuation signal.

AREA, BUILDING. The area included within surrounding exterior walls (or exterior walls and firewalls) exclusive of vent shafts and courts. Areas of the building not provided with surrounding walls shall be included in the building area if such areas are included within the horizontal projection of the roof or floor above. CONSTRUCTION. The excavation, erection, alteration, and repair of buildings or any component parts, including all operations incidental thereto. DWELLING. A building or structure that is occupied in whole or in part as the home, residence or sleeping place of one or more families. EMERGENCY VOICE/ALARM COMMUNICATIONS. Dedicated manual or automatic facilities for originating and distributing voice instructions, as well as alert and evacuation signals pertaining to a fire or other emergency, to the occupants of a building. FIRE ALARM SYSTEM . A system or portion of a combination system consisting of components and circuits arranged to monitor and annunciate the status of fire alarm or supervisory signal - initiating devices and to initiate the appropriate response to those signals . FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM. Approved devices, equipment and systems or combinations of systems used to detect a fire, activate an alarm, extinguish or control a fire, control or manage smoke and products of a fire or any combination thereof. NEW CONSTRUCTION. See Section G201.1.2. SMOKE. Air-borne solid and liquid particulates and gases evolved when a material undergoes pyrolysis or combustion, including the quality of air that is entrained or otherwise mixed into the mass.

In cases where changes in the scope of work during the course of construction would result in increasing the floor surface area at the completion of construction by more than 110 percent, over the amount of existing floor surface area as determined pursuant to section 28-101.4.5 , such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if hereafter erected and such work shall be refiled as a new building application in accordance with the provisions of section 28-105.2 . testCase.question: A small existing establishment proposes an alteration described as a change between Group B and Group M after the 2024 zoning Use Group renumbering. Based only on the selected Building Code passages, can we conclude that the work qualifies for an exception to amending the Certificate of Occupancy, and what accessibility consequence can be stated?
testCase.expectedConclusion: No Certificate of Occupancy exception can be established from the selected evidence. BC 1101.3 addresses accessibility in alterations and changes of use or occupancy in prior-code buildings; it is not the authority for a Certificate of Occupancy amendment exception. If the project is an alteration in a prior-code building and is considered a change in the space's Building Code occupancy classification or zoning use group, BC 1101.3.1 conditionally requires the Chapter 11 accessible features and construction throughout the space, including its immediate entrances. The existing Certificate of Occupancy, the actual former and current zoning uses under the applicable transition rule, the Building Code classifications, and the governing Administrative Code and official agency material must be reviewed before deciding either the Certificate of Occupancy issue or whether this accessibility trigger applies.

answer.answerText:
No. The selected Building Code passages do not address amendment of a Certificate of Occupancy or establish an exception from that process. They therefore cannot support a conclusion that the proposed B/M change qualifies for a Certificate-of-Occupancy exception. The applicable Administrative Code Certificate-of-Occupancy provision and the text of any claimed exception are needed to evaluate that separate issue.

The accessibility consequence is conditional. If the building is a prior-code building and the work is an alteration rather than an ordinary repair, Chapter 11 applies. Where that alteration is considered either a change in Building Code occupancy classification or a change in zoning use group under the Zoning Resolution, Chapter 11 accessible features and construction must be provided throughout the space, including its immediate entrance(s).

The selected passages do not establish whether the stated B/M change is an actual Building Code occupancy-classification change, whether the 2024 zoning renumbering results in a zoning-use-group change for this space, or which particular Chapter 11 features are required.

2. So as to obstruct any exit from a building;

testCase.question: A restaurant proposes a sidewalk café with furniture near a building exit and cellar hatch. The owner says outdoor-dining authorization allows the exterior seats to be counted separately from the interior PACO and eliminates further accessibility review. The documents do not say whether the café is beyond the building line, enclosed, or separated from the interior seating by a Section 713 fire partition. What can be concluded from the selected Building Code passages, and what remains unresolved?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The proposal cannot be approved from the selected evidence. If it is a sidewalk café beyond the building line, BC 3111.1 requires compliance not only with Section 3111 but also with Chapter 32 and separate zoning and agency requirements; the selected evidence does not provide those outside rules. BC 3111.4 prohibits café components from obstructing a building exit or cellar hatch. Its cellar-entrance exception is not automatic: it requires a special application, an easily removable and prominently designated platform designed under Section 3111.5, and a cellar entrance or areaway that is not required egress. BC 3111.6 makes Chapter 11 applicable to the café and its access. BC 1108.2.9.1 requires accessible seating and standing spaces equal to at least 10 percent of the total, with not less than one accessible space at each type of dining surface; those spaces must be distributed and located on a level served by an accessible route. BC 3111.7 supplies only a conditional rule for an enclosed sidewalk café: unless a Section 713 fire partition separates it from inside seating, its seating is added to the inside seating solely to determine whether a PACO is required. These passages do not establish the approved interior capacity, the treatment of every open exterior seating arrangement, property-line or operational jurisdiction, current agency authorization, or overall approval.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages establish several conditional Building Code constraints, but they do not establish overall approval, current agency jurisdiction, or lawful seating capacity.

answer.answerText:
The owner’s position is not established by these passages. If the proposed sidewalk café is beyond the building line, BC 3111.1 requires compliance not only with BC 3111 but also with the Zoning Resolution, the requirements of the Commissioners of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and Department of Transportation, and Chapter 32 projection limitations. An asserted outdoor-dining authorization therefore does not, on this evidence, eliminate Building Code accessibility review.

The café furniture, equipment, enclosure, removable platform, and similar components may not obstruct a building exit, cellar access hatch, or areaway. A platform over a cellar entrance or areaway is allowed only if the commissioner permits it upon special application and it is easily removable, prominently designated, designed under BC 3111.5, and covers an entrance/areaway not used as a required means of egress. The supplied record does not establish compliance because the exit and hatch geometry, hatch use, and any special approval are unknown.

Accessibility remains required: the sidewalk café and its access must comply with Chapter 11. Where dining surfaces are provided, at least 10 percent of total seating and standing spaces must be accessible, with at least one accessible seating or standing space at each type of dining surface; those accessible surfaces must be distributed throughout the facility and be on a level accessed by an accessible route. The 10-percent requirement applies to the total number of seating and standing spaces, while the minimum of one applies separately to each dining-surface type. The proposed seating counts, surface types, accessible-surface distribution, and accessible-route conditions are not provided, so a numerical/accessibility compliance finding cannot be made.

Separate exterior seating cannot be assumed for the place-of-assembly certificate-of-operation determination. For an enclosed sidewalk café, its seating must be added to interior seating unless the two are separated by fire partitions complying with Section 713. Because enclosure status and the presence and compliance of any Section 713 fire partition are unknown, the supplied evidence does not establish whether exterior seating may be excluded from that combined count. This passage addresses whether a place-of-assembly certificate of operation is required; it does not establish a general right to treat exterior seats separately for every code purpose.
answer.conclusion: The owner’s position is not established by these passages. If the proposed sidewalk café is beyond the building line, BC 3111.1 requires compliance not only with BC 3111 but also with the Zoning Resolution, the requirements of the Commissioners of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and Department of Transportation, and Chapter 32 projection limitations. An asserted outdoor-dining authorization therefore does not, on this evidence, eliminate Building Code accessibility review.

The exact building-line location is therefore material to applying this provision.

supportedPoints.heading: Café components cannot obstruct exits or cellar access
supportedPoints.explanation: No awning, enclosure, fixture, equipment, removable platform, or other listed sidewalk-café component may obstruct a building exit, cellar access hatch, or areaway. A commissioner may, upon special application, permit an easily removable, prominently designated platform designed under Section 3111.5 to cover a cellar entrance or areaway only when it is not used as a required means of egress.

supportedPoints.heading: Sidewalk cafés remain subject to accessibility requirements
supportedPoints.explanation: Sidewalk cafés and their access must comply with Chapter 11. Where dining surfaces are provided for food or drink consumption, at least 10 percent of total seating and standing spaces must be accessible; at least one of each type of dining surface must be accessible; and accessible surfaces must be distributed throughout the facility and located on a level accessed by an accessible route.

supportedPoints.heading: Enclosed café seating is generally combined with interior seating for the stated certificate determination
supportedPoints.explanation: For an enclosed sidewalk café, seating must be added to seating inside the building to determine whether a place-of-assembly certificate of operation is required, unless the seating areas are separated by fire partitions complying with Section 713.

exactPassages: Where mechanical ventilation systems for enclosed parking garages operate intermittently, such operation shall be automatic by means of carbon monoxide detectors applied in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors.
Such detectors shall be installed in accordance with their manufacturers' instructions.

testCase.question: An enclosed parking garage will use intermittent mechanical ventilation. The proposed controls use carbon monoxide detectors only and start the system at 35 ppm carbon monoxide. Based only on the selected Mechanical Code provision, is that control sequence compliant, and what can and cannot be concluded?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The proposed control sequence does not match MC 404.1. For intermittent operation in an enclosed parking garage, automatic operation must use carbon monoxide detectors in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors. The system must operate automatically when carbon monoxide reaches 25 ppm or nitrogen dioxide reaches 500 ppb, so a carbon-monoxide-only sequence at 35 ppm omits the required nitrogen dioxide detection and exceeds the stated carbon monoxide trigger. The detectors must also be installed according to their manufacturers' instructions. The selected provision does not establish detector quantity or placement, the complete ventilation rate and capacity, or compliance of the rest of the mechanical design.

answer.answerText:
No. Based on the selected MC 404.1 text, the proposed CO-only, 35-ppm sequence is not compliant for an intermittently operated mechanical ventilation system in an enclosed parking garage.

The system must operate automatically through carbon monoxide detectors used in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors. It must start automatically when either CO reaches 25 ppm or NO₂ reaches 500 ppb. A 35-ppm CO start point is above the stated 25-ppm trigger, and CO detectors alone do not satisfy the required conjunction with NO₂ detectors. The detectors also must be installed under their manufacturers’ instructions.

This conclusion is limited to the stated control sequence under the selected provision. The supplied text does not establish whether the proposed detector quantity, locations, or coverage comply with manufacturer instructions; whether another proposed sequence supplies the required NO₂ detection and 25-ppm/500-ppb automatic operation; or whether the ventilation airflow rate and system capacity comply with other Mechanical Code requirements.

exactPassages: Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. See section 28-105.2 for permits for such work.
Exceptions. When determining the amount of existing floor surface area for the purposes of section 28-101.4.5 , the following shall be excluded from the measured square footage of floor surface area:
1. The square footage of floors removed during the course of the work when such floors are removed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade.

2. The square footage of any floor that was installed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade less than 12 months prior to submission of the application for construction document approval for the proposed work. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

testCase.question: A prior-code building was filed as an alteration based on a 105 percent floor-surface-area increase, but scope changes during construction may raise the increase to 115 percent. Can the project remain an alteration, what happens if the threshold is crossed, and what must be included or excluded when checking the percentage?
testCase.expectedConclusion: If verified scope changes increase floor surface area at completion by more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area as determined under AC 28-101.4.5, AC 28-101.4.5.1 requires the entire building to comply as if newly erected and requires the work to be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. The narrow emergency exception allows only work necessary to relieve an emergency condition before plans are amended or a new permit is obtained. AC 28-101.4.5.2 defines floor surface area as the gross area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces at every level, expressly including bulkhead and superstructure roofs, cellar, attic, and roof. When measuring existing floor surface area, AC 28-101.4.5 excludes qualifying floors removed with their supporting construction and qualifying floors installed with their supporting construction less than 12 months before the filing. The stated 105 and 115 percent estimates are not enough without verified measurements, dates, removed-floor scope, and filing facts.

answer.answerText:
No—if the corrected calculation shows that the changed work will increase the building’s floor surface area at completion by more than 110% over the statutorily determined existing floor surface area, the project cannot remain under the prior-code alteration authorization. At the stated 115%, it crosses that threshold, subject to verifying the required area basis. The entire building must comply with the current code as if newly erected, and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. This rule expressly applies to scope changes made during construction. By contrast, exactly 110% does not satisfy a trigger stated as more than 110%.

For this comparison, floor surface area means the gross square footage of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces at every level, including cellar, attic, roof, and roofs of bulkheads and superstructures. When determining the existing-area amount, exclude: (1) a floor removed during the work only if it is removed together with its supporting beams, joists, decking, and slabs on grade; and (2) a floor installed with that supporting construction less than 12 months before submission of the construction-document-approval application. A floor installed under a work permit signed off less than 12 months before that submission also is not counted as existing floor surface area. These exclusions reduce the existing-area base and can increase the resulting percentage.

The emergency exception is limited: work necessary to relieve an emergency condition may proceed before plans are amended or a new permit is obtained. It does not eliminate the refiling and whole-building new-building compliance consequence once the more-than-110% threshold is met.
answer.conclusion: No—if the corrected calculation shows that the changed work will increase the building’s floor surface area at completion by more than 110% over the statutorily determined existing floor surface area, the project cannot remain under the prior-code alteration authorization. At the stated 115%, it crosses that threshold, subject to verifying the required area basis. The entire building must comply with the current code as if newly erected, and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. This rule expressly applies to scope changes made during construction. By contrast, exactly 110% does not satisfy a trigger stated as more than 110%.

supportedPoints.heading: Construction-phase scope changes require refiling
supportedPoints.explanation: If a change in scope during construction would result in a more-than-110% increase, using existing floor surface area determined under AC 28-101.4.5, the entire building must comply as if newly erected and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2.

supportedPoints.heading: Required exclusions from existing area
